claim: Two to three laminar probes (each with 16 recording contacts spaced along the recording shaft) were used to simultaneously record from cortical area V1 of two macaques (M1 and M2).
source: We recorded simultaneously from two to three laminar probes (each with 16 recording contacts spaced along the recording shaft, see Supplementary Materials for alignment procedure) in cortical area V1 of two macaques (M1 and M2) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Distances between probes of 1–6 mm were used, matching approximately the extent of V1 horizontal connectivity.
source: We used distances between probes of 1–6 mm, matching approximately the extent of V1 horizontal connectivity (Stettler et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement describes the experimental design and cites a reference for the extent of V1 horizontal connectivity.

claim: Horizontal connectivity strength declines strongly with distance between cortical locations.
source: Notably, horizontal connectivity strength declines strongly with distance between cortical locations (Stettler et al., 2002), so that increasing inter-probe distance indexes decreasing horizontal connectivity strength.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stettler et al., 2002.

claim: Increasing inter-probe distance indexes decreasing horizontal connectivity strength.
source: Notably, horizontal connectivity strength declines strongly with distance between cortical locations (Stettler et al., 2002), so that increasing inter-probe distance indexes decreasing horizontal connectivity strength.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited relationship between distance and connectivity strength.

claim: The monkeys fixated centrally while a full-screen static square-wave grating with spatially varying contrast was shown.
source: The monkeys fixated centrally while a full-screen static square-wave grating with spatially varying contrast was shown (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental paradigm used in the study.

claim: The local contrast varied periodically over visual space such that different contrasts were presented to different cortical locations.
source: The local contrast varied periodically over visual space such that different contrasts were presented to different cortical locations.
evidence: This describes the stimulus design used in the experiment.

claim: The magnitude of contrast difference ranged from 0% to ~43%.
source: The magnitude of contrast difference (ranging from 0% to ~43%, see Table S1) was manipulated by varying the sign and amplitude of the spatial variation in contrast.
evidence: This describes the range of contrast differences used in the experiment.

claim: The stimulus gratings induced gamma power in layers 2–4 and in the deepest layer.
source: The stimulus gratings induced gamma power in layers 2–4 and in the deepest layer (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014; Xing et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in figures and citations to previous studies.

claim: The gamma frequency increased systematically with higher local contrast in monkey M1 (linear regression, single contact level, R2 = 0.38, p<10−10).
source: The gamma frequency increased systematically with higher local contrast (linear regression, single contact level, M1: R2 = 0.38, M2: R2 = 0.27, both p<10−10, Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The gamma frequency increased systematically with higher local contrast in monkey M2 (linear regression, single contact level, R2 = 0.27, p<10−10).
source: The gamma frequency increased systematically with higher local contrast (linear regression, single contact level, M1: R2 = 0.38, M2: R2 = 0.27, both p<10−10, Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The range of the frequency shift in the data was ~5 Hz.
source: The range of the frequency shift in our data (~5 Hz) was smaller than in Roberts et al., 2013, reflecting a narrower contrast range used here; from ~20% to ~60% (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the observed frequency shift range in the current study.

claim: The range of the frequency shift was smaller than in Roberts et al., 2013, reflecting a narrower contrast range used in the current study.
source: The range of the frequency shift in our data (~5 Hz) was smaller than in Roberts et al., 2013, reflecting a narrower contrast range used here; from ~20% to ~60% (Table 1).
evidence: This is a comparison with a previous study and an explanation for the difference.

claim: The tight relationship between contrast and gamma frequency allowed induction of different mean frequencies in nearby cortical locations separated by as little as 1–6 mm.
source: The tight relationship between contrast and gamma frequency allowed us to induce different mean frequencies in nearby cortical locations separated by as little as 1–6 mm (e.g., Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed relationship between contrast and frequency.

claim: The instantaneous frequency difference changed as a function of phase difference.
source: However, the frequency difference was not constant. Instead, the instantaneous frequency difference changed as a function of phase difference (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) with a modulation amplitude of ~1 Hz (approximately (max-min)/2; see Appendix).
evidence: This describes a key observation from the data analysis.

claim: The modulation amplitude of instantaneous frequency difference was ~1 Hz in the first example.
source: However, the frequency difference was not constant. Instead, the instantaneous frequency difference changed as a function of phase difference (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) with a modulation amplitude of ~1 Hz (approximately (max-min)/2; see Appendix).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data.

claim: At the smallest frequency difference (4 Hz), the phase precession was slowest (2π every 250 ms).
source: At the smallest frequency difference (4 Hz, yellow point), the phase precession was slowest (2π every 250 ms).
evidence: This describes a specific observation from the data.

claim: The probability distribution of phase differences over time gave a phase-locking value (PLV) of 0.11 in the first example.
source: As a result, the probability distribution of phase differences over time (Figure 3C) was non-uniform giving a phase-locking value (Lachaux et al., 1999) (PLV) of 0.11.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data.

claim: The peak of the phase difference distribution was at 1.3 rad in the first example.
source: The peak of the distribution, the 'preferred phase', was at 1.3 rad, in line with the minimum of the instantaneous frequency modulation shape.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data.

claim: In the second example, the instantaneous frequency modulation was larger with a modulation amplitude of 1.8 Hz.
source: The instantaneous frequency modulation was larger with a modulation amplitude of 1.8 Hz (Figure 3E) and a minimum around 3 Hz at the preferred phase.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data.

claim: The second example resulted in a narrower phase difference distribution, indicating higher synchrony (PLV = 0.32).
source: This resulted in a narrower phase difference distribution, indicating higher synchrony (PLV = 0.32, Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data.

claim: The peak of the phase difference distribution was centered at a smaller phase difference (0.78 rad) in the second example.
source: The peak of the distribution was centered at a smaller phase difference (0.78 rad).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data.

claim: In the third example, the magnitude of the instantaneous frequency modulation did not change (modulation amplitude 1.8 Hz) compared to example 2.
source: Compared to example 2, the magnitude of the instantaneous frequency modulation did not change (modulation amplitude 1.8 Hz, Figure 3H), but showed a lower mean difference and a minimum close to zero (1 Hz, Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a comparison of quantitative measurements from the data.

claim: The third example showed a lower mean frequency difference and a minimum close to zero (1 Hz).
source: Compared to example 2, the magnitude of the instantaneous frequency modulation did not change (modulation amplitude 1.8 Hz, Figure 3H), but showed a lower mean difference and a minimum close to zero (1 Hz, Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data.

claim: The phase difference probability distribution became even more pronounced and narrower (PLV = 0.51) in the third example.
source: Thus, the associated phase difference (0.48 rad) could be maintained for even longer periods and the phase difference probability distribution became even more pronounced and narrower (PLV = 0.51, Figure 3I).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data.

claim: The three examples illustrate how the mean frequency difference and cortical distance determine the dynamic relationship between the instantaneous frequency difference and the phase difference during synchronization.
source: The three examples illustrate how the mean frequency difference and cortical distance (a proxy of the strength of horizontal interactions) determine the dynamic relationship between the instantaneous frequency difference and the phase difference during synchronization.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the implications of the three examples.

claim: The dataset comprised 805 recorded across-probe contact pairs in monkey M1.
source: In the following sections, we will show how these observations were characteristic of the whole dataset comprising 805 recorded across-probe contact pairs in monkey M1 and 882 pairs in monkey M2.
evidence: This describes the size of the dataset.

claim: The dataset comprised 882 recorded across-probe contact pairs in monkey M2.
source: In the following sections, we will show how these observations were characteristic of the whole dataset comprising 805 recorded across-probe contact pairs in monkey M1 and 882 pairs in monkey M2.
evidence: This describes the size of the dataset.

claim: The interaction function G(θ) was estimated as being approximately a sinusoidal function.
source: The interaction function G(θ) was estimated as being approximately a sinusoidal function (Figure 6B) with relatively symmetric negative and positive components (Akam et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the estimated shape of the interaction function from the data.

claim: The interaction function G(θ) had relatively symmetric negative and positive components.
source: The interaction function G(θ) was estimated as being approximately a sinusoidal function (Figure 6B) with relatively symmetric negative and positive components (Akam et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes a property of the estimated interaction function.

claim: The phase noise parameter σ was found to be 19 Hz in monkey M1.
source: The phase noise parameter σ was found to be relatively large (M1: σ = 19 Hz, M2: σ = 20 Hz) indicating substantial frequency variability not explained by the interaction function (likely due to inherent noise and interactions with other cortical locations).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data analysis.

claim: The phase noise parameter σ was found to be 20 Hz in monkey M2.
source: The phase noise parameter σ was found to be relatively large (M1: σ = 19 Hz, M2: σ = 20 Hz) indicating substantial frequency variability not explained by the interaction function (likely due to inherent noise and interactions with other cortical locations).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data analysis.

claim: The phase noise parameter σ indicates substantial frequency variability not explained by the interaction function.
source: The phase noise parameter σ was found to be relatively large (M1: σ = 19 Hz, M2: σ = 20 Hz) indicating substantial frequency variability not explained by the interaction function (likely due to inherent noise and interactions with other cortical locations).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the phase noise parameter value.

claim: The detuning ∆ω was positively correlated with the local contrast difference in monkey M1 (linear regression, R2 = 0.28, p<10−10).
source: The detuning ∆ω was positively correlated with the local contrast difference (linear regression, M1: R2 = 0.28, M2: R2 = 0.25, both p<10−10) and with MUA rate difference between probes (linear regression, M1: R2 = 0.53, M2: R2 = 0.36, both p<10−10) in line with Ray and Maunsell, 2010.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result from the data.

claim: The detuning ∆ω was positively correlated with the local contrast difference in monkey M2 (linear regression, R2 = 0.25, p<10−10).
source: The detuning ∆ω was positively correlated with the local contrast difference (linear regression, M1: R2 = 0.28, M2: R2 = 0.25, both p<10−10) and with MUA rate difference between probes (linear regression, M1: R2 = 0.53, M2: R2 = 0.36, both p<10−10) in line with Ray and Maunsell, 2010.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result from the data.

claim: The detuning ∆ω was positively correlated with MUA rate difference between probes in monkey M1 (linear regression, R2 = 0.53, p<10−10).
source: The detuning ∆ω was positively correlated with the local contrast difference (linear regression, M1: R2 = 0.28, M2: R2 = 0.25, both p<10−10) and with MUA rate difference between probes (linear regression, M1: R2 = 0.53, M2: R2 = 0.36, both p<10−10) in line with Ray and Maunsell, 2010.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result from the data.

claim: The detuning ∆ω was positively correlated with MUA rate difference between probes in monkey M2 (linear regression, R2 = 0.36, p<10−10).
source: The detuning ∆ω was positively correlated with the local contrast difference (linear regression, M1: R2 = 0.28, M2: R2 = 0.25, both p<10−10) and with MUA rate difference between probes (linear regression, M1: R2 = 0.53, M2: R2 = 0.36, both p<10−10) in line with Ray and Maunsell, 2010.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result from the data.

claim: The interaction strength ε was inversely correlated with the cortical distance between probes in monkey M1 (linear regression, R2 = 0.41, p<10−10).
source: The interaction strength ε was found to be inversely correlated with the cortical distance between probes (linear regression, M1: R2 = 0.41, M2: R2 = 0.29, both p<10−10, Figure 6C), in line with the known decrease of V1 horizontal connectivity with distance (Stettler et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result from the data.

claim: The interaction strength ε was inversely correlated with the cortical distance between probes in monkey M2 (linear regression, R2 = 0.29, p<10−10).
source: The interaction strength ε was found to be inversely correlated with the cortical distance between probes (linear regression, M1: R2 = 0.41, M2: R2 = 0.29, both p<10−10, Figure 6C), in line with the known decrease of V1 horizontal connectivity with distance (Stettler et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result from the data.

claim: The inverse correlation between interaction strength ε and cortical distance is in line with the known decrease of V1 horizontal connectivity with distance.
source: The interaction strength ε was found to be inversely correlated with the cortical distance between probes (linear regression, M1: R2 = 0.41, M2: R2 = 0.29, both p<10−10, Figure 6C), in line with the known decrease of V1 horizontal connectivity with distance (Stettler et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation result in the context of known anatomy.

claim: Gamma PLV variations over single contact pairs were significantly captured by the analytical predictions as a function of ∆ω and ε in monkey M1 (model accuracy: R2 = 0.18, n = 7245).
source: We found that the gamma PLV variations over single contact pairs were significantly captured by the analytical predictions as a function of ∆ω and ε (model accuracy: M1: R2 = 0.18, n = 7245, M2: R2 = 0.32, n = 7938, Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing model predictions to data.

claim: Gamma PLV variations over single contact pairs were significantly captured by the analytical predictions as a function of ∆ω and ε in monkey M2 (model accuracy: R2 = 0.32, n = 7938).
source: We found that the gamma PLV variations over single contact pairs were significantly captured by the analytical predictions as a function of ∆ω and ε (model accuracy: M1: R2 = 0.18, n = 7245, M2: R2 = 0.32, n = 7938, Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing model predictions to data.

claim: The model predicted variation of PLV evaluated for each single contact pair separately in monkey M1 (model accuracy: R2 = 0.27 ± 0.0002, n = 802).
source: We also tested whether the model predicted variation of PLV evaluated for each single contact pair separately, where variation is induced mainly by detuning (model accuracy: M1: R2 = 0.27 ± 0.0002, n = 802, M2: R2 = 0.1 ± 0.0001, n = 882).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing model predictions to data.

claim: The model predicted variation of PLV evaluated for each single contact pair separately in monkey M2 (model accuracy: R2 = 0.1 ± 0.0001, n = 882).
source: We also tested whether the model predicted variation of PLV evaluated for each single contact pair separately, where variation is induced mainly by detuning (model accuracy: M1: R2 = 0.27 ± 0.0002, n = 802, M2: R2 = 0.1 ± 0.0001, n = 882).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing model predictions to data.

claim: The population means of PLV were very well predicted by the model in monkey M1 (model accuracy: R2 = 0.83, n = 638).
source: The population means, defined as the averaged PLV values of contacts pairs with a similar detuning and cortical distance (bin size: ±0.35 Hz, ±0.3 mm), were very well predicted (model accuracy: M1: R2 = 0.83, M2: R2 = 0.86, both n = 638).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing model predictions to data.

claim: The population means of PLV were very well predicted by the model in monkey M2 (model accuracy: R2 = 0.86, n = 638).
source: The population means, defined as the averaged PLV values of contacts pairs with a similar detuning and cortical distance (bin size: ±0.35 Hz, ±0.3 mm), were very well predicted (model accuracy: M1: R2 = 0.83, M2: R2 = 0.86, both n = 638).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing model predictions to data.

claim: A positive phase difference (phase X – phase Y) means that contact X leads (precedes in time) contact Y in terms of the phase of its oscillatory activity.
source: A positive phase difference (phase X – phase Y) means that contact X leads (precedes in time) contact Y in terms of the phase of its oscillatory activity.
evidence: This is a definition of the phase difference measure used.

claim: The phase difference ranged nearly between –pi/2 to pi/2 in both M1 and M2.
source: The phase difference ranged nearly between –pi/2 to pi/2 in both M1 and M2.
evidence: This describes the range of observed phase differences.

claim: Single contact pair data for mean phase difference was substantially captured by the analytical predictions as a function of ∆ω and ε in monkey M1 (model accuracy: R2 = 0.56, n = 7245).
source: Again, single contact pair data was substantially captured by the analytical predictions as a function of ∆ω and ε (model accuracy: M1: R2 = 0.56, n = 7245, M2: R2 = 0.3, n=7938 Figure 6H,I).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing model predictions to data.

claim: Single contact pair data for mean phase difference was substantially captured by the analytical predictions as a function of ∆ω and ε in monkey M2 (model accuracy: R2 = 0.3, n = 7938).
source: Again, single contact pair data was substantially captured by the analytical predictions as a function of ∆ω and ε (model accuracy: M1: R2 = 0.56, n = 7245, M2: R2 = 0.3, n=7938 Figure 6H,I).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing model predictions to data.

claim: The model predicted variability of phase difference evaluated for each single contact pair separately in monkey M1 (model accuracy: R2 = 0.52 ± 0.0002, n = 802).
source: Furthermore, we tested whether the model predicted variability of phase difference evaluated for each single contact pair separately. This variability mainly represents variability induced specifically by detuning (model accuracy: M1: R2 = 0.52 ± 0.0002, n = 802, M2: R2 = 0.44 ± 0.0004, n = 882).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing model predictions to data.

claim: The model predicted variability of phase difference evaluated for each single contact pair separately in monkey M2 (model accuracy: R2 = 0.44 ± 0.0004, n = 882).
source: Furthermore, we tested whether the model predicted variability of phase difference evaluated for each single contact pair separately. This variability mainly represents variability induced specifically by detuning (model accuracy: M1: R2 = 0.52 ± 0.0002, n = 802, M2: R2 = 0.44 ± 0.0004, n = 882).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing model predictions to data.

claim: The observed population means for mean phase difference followed the analytical predictions precisely in monkey M1 (model accuracy: R2 = 0.92, n = 638).
source: The observed population means for different ∆ω and ε values followed the analytical predictions precisely (model accuracy: M1: R2 = 0.92, M2: R2 = 0.88, both n = 638).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing model predictions to data.

claim: The observed population means for mean phase difference followed the analytical predictions precisely in monkey M2 (model accuracy: R2 = 0.88, n = 638).
source: The observed population means for different ∆ω and ε values followed the analytical predictions precisely (model accuracy: M1: R2 = 0.92, M2: R2 = 0.88, both n = 638).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing model predictions to data.

claim: The gamma rhythm with the higher frequency in a pair had the leading phase.
source: The gamma rhythm with the higher frequency in a pair had the leading phase and the mean phase difference increased with increased detuning.
evidence: This describes a relationship observed in the data.

claim: The mean phase difference increased with increased detuning.
source: The gamma rhythm with the higher frequency in a pair had the leading phase and the mean phase difference increased with increased detuning.
evidence: This describes a relationship observed in the data.

claim: This is the first demonstration that phase locking values and preferred phase differences in primate cortex can be quantitatively predicted based on theoretical principles and limited knowledge of the system.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that phase locking values and preferred phase differences in primate cortex can be quantitatively predicted based on theoretical principles and limited knowledge of the system.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Observed CSD-CSD gamma PLVs in V1 as a function of ∆ω and ε revealed a structure that fitted the predicted Arnold tongue in both monkeys.
source: Figure 7A shows the observed PLV (color-coded) plotted as a function of ∆ω and ε, revealing a structure that fitted the predicted Arnold tongue in both monkeys.
evidence: This describes the observation of the Arnold tongue structure in the data.

claim: Conditions of high interaction strength and low detuning showed strong gamma synchronization.
source: As predicted, conditions of high interaction strength and low detuning showed strong gamma synchronization, whereas conditions of low interaction strength and high detuning yielded weak gamma synchronization.
evidence: This describes the pattern of synchronization observed in the Arnold tongue.

claim: Conditions of low interaction strength and high detuning yielded weak gamma synchronization.
source: As predicted, conditions of high interaction strength and low detuning showed strong gamma synchronization, whereas conditions of low interaction strength and high detuning yielded weak gamma synchronization.
evidence: This describes the pattern of synchronization observed in the Arnold tongue.

claim: A model consisting of two coupled PING networks yielded the Arnold tongue when interaction strength was manipulated by changing synaptic connectivity between the networks, and detuning by imposing differential excitatory drive.
source: Notably, a model consisting of two coupled PING networks, in which interaction strength was manipulated by changing synaptic connectivity between the networks, and detuning by imposing differential excitatory drive, also yielded the Arnold tongue (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a modeling result that supports the empirical findings.

claim: CSD-CSD analysis between deep contacts (L5-6) confirmed a similar Arnold tongue structure.
source: CSD-CSD analysis between deep contacts (L5-6) confirmed a similar Arnold tongue structure showing that the Arnold tongue properties do apply across the cortical layers.
evidence: This describes an additional analysis confirming the Arnold tongue across cortical layers.

claim: The Arnold tongue properties apply across the cortical layers.
source: CSD-CSD analysis between deep contacts (L5-6) confirmed a similar Arnold tongue structure showing that the Arnold tongue properties do apply across the cortical layers.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of deep layer contacts.

claim: V1-V2 pairs exhibited similar phase-dependent instantaneous frequency modulations.
source: We tested for V1-V2 pairs whether they exhibited similar phase-dependent instantaneous frequency modulations. We found that this was indeed the case (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes an additional analysis of V1-V2 interactions.

claim: The systematic variation of the phase difference between contact pairs by detuning indicates that detuning can affect the information flow between gamma rhythms.
source: The systematic variation of the phase difference between contact pairs by detuning indicates that detuning can affect the information flow between gamma rhythms (Besserve et al., 2015; Buehlmann and Deco, 2010; Cannon et al., 2014; Lowet et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference from the observed relationship between detuning and phase difference, supported by citations.

claim: Spikes from a neural rhythm that leads another neural rhythm in time are more effective.
source: This is because spikes from a neural rhythm that leads another neural rhythm in time are more effective (Buehlmann and Deco, 2010; Cannon et al., 2014; Fries, 2015).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A change in the sign of detuning and phase difference was linked to a change in the direction of strongest granger causality.
source: We observed that a change in the sign of detuning and phase difference was linked to a change in the direction of strongest granger causality (Figure 8).
evidence: This describes a relationship observed in the Granger causality analysis.

claim: Gamma (instantaneous) amplitude varied weakly or moderately as a function of phase difference in experimental V1 data.
source: We observed one property of synchronization that was not accounted by the model equations. We found that gamma (instantaneous) amplitude (the absolute of analytical signal) varied weakly or moderately as a function of phase difference (Figure 7—figure supplement 4) in our experimental V1 data
evidence: This describes an observation not captured by the model.

claim: Gamma amplitude variations were replicated in simulation data of two mutually coupled PING spiking networks.
source: These amplitude variations were replicated also in simulation data of two mutually coupled PING spiking networks.
evidence: This describes a modeling result that replicates the empirical observation.

claim: The gamma amplitude variation became stronger with interaction strength.
source: The gamma amplitude variation became stronger with interaction strength.
evidence: This describes a relationship observed in the data.

claim: Increased mutual entrainment of synchronizing local gamma rhythms can enhance their amplitudes.
source: It has been shown before that increased mutual entrainment of synchronizing local gamma rhythms can enhance their amplitudes (Womelsdorf et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: TWCO remains highly predictive even in conditions of weak-to-moderate amplitude variations as long these variations do not strongly change the phase trajectory.
source: However, TWCO remains highly predictive even in conditions of weak-to-moderate amplitude variations as long these variations do not strongly change the phase trajectory (Izhikevich, 2007; Kopell and Ermentrout, 2002; Pikovsky et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about the applicability of TWCO, supported by citations.

claim: Anatomical coupling is an important factor defining the interaction strength.
source: We propose that anatomical coupling is an important factor defining the interaction strength, however by itself is not sufficient to fully predict the amount of functional gamma-band interactions.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the findings.

claim: Anatomical coupling by itself is not sufficient to fully predict the amount of functional gamma-band interactions.
source: We propose that anatomical coupling is an important factor defining the interaction strength, however by itself is not sufficient to fully predict the amount of functional gamma-band interactions.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the findings.

claim: The amount of detuning can functionally couple or decouple anatomically connected cortical locations.
source: Critical in addition is the amount of detuning that can functionally couple or decouple anatomically connected cortical locations.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the findings.

claim: Gamma synchronization in awake monkey V1 adheres to theoretical principles of weakly coupled oscillators.
source: The present study shows that gamma synchronization in awake monkey V1 adheres to theoretical principles of weakly coupled oscillators (Ermentrout and Kleinfeld, 2001; Hoppensteadt and Izhikevich, 1998; Kopell and Ermentrout, 2002; Kuramoto, 1991; Pikovsky et al., 2002; Winfree, 1967), thereby providing insight into the synchronization regime of gamma rhythms and its principles.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding, supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: The synchronization principles are likely to also apply to other brain regions and frequency bands.
source: Given the generality of the synchronization principles, they are likely to also apply to other brain regions and frequency bands.
evidence: This is a speculation about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: Phase-dependent frequency modulations show that a fixed and common frequency is not required for phase coordination.
source: Our findings reveal the importance of phase-dependent frequency modulations for synchronizing V1 gamma rhythms. These modulations show that a fixed and common frequency is not required for phase coordination.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Stronger non-stationary frequency modulations led to stronger synchronization.
source: To the contrary, stronger non-stationary frequency modulations led to stronger synchronization, and thus to more reliable phase coordination.
evidence: This describes a relationship observed in the data.

claim: Frequency modulations arise naturally in the intermittent synchronization regime.
source: Frequency modulations arise naturally in the intermittent synchronization regime (Ermentrout and Rinzel, 1984b; Izhikevich, 2007; Pikovsky et al., 2002), when oscillators cannot remain in a stable equilibrium due to detuning and noise.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical basis for frequency modulations, supported by citations.

claim: Intermittent synchronization is the most likely regime for phase coordination of gamma rhythms in vivo.
source: Given the variable nature of gamma rhythms in vivo (Atallah and Scanziani, 2009; Burns et al., 2010; Ray and Maunsell, 2010; Roberts et al., 2013), intermittent synchronization is the most likely regime for their phase coordination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the variable nature of gamma rhythms and the theory of intermittent synchronization.

claim: Phase coordination remains sufficiently robust to influence the strength and directionality of information flow in the intermittent synchronization regime.
source: Although complete synchronization is not achieved in this regime, phase coordination remains sufficiently robust to influence the strength and directionality of information flow, by rendering particular phase-relations more likely than others (Battaglia et al., 2012; Buehlmann and Deco, 2010; Fries, 2015; Maris et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the functional implications of intermittent synchronization, supported by citations.

claim: The observation of non-stationary frequency modulations has methodological implications.
source: The observation of non-stationary frequency modulations also has methodological implications.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings for methodology.

claim: Gamma rhythms are often studied with stationary methods, for example spectral coherence or stationary Granger measures.
source: Gamma rhythms are often studied with stationary methods, for example spectral coherence or stationary Granger measures, yet our findings are not in line with the (weak-sense) stationarity assumption (Lachaux et al., 1999; Lowet et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about current methodological practices, supported by citations.

claim: The findings are not in line with the (weak-sense) stationarity assumption.
source: Gamma rhythms are often studied with stationary methods, for example spectral coherence or stationary Granger measures, yet our findings are not in line with the (weak-sense) stationarity assumption (Lachaux et al., 1999; Lowet et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings for the stationarity assumption.

claim: Time-resolved non-stationary methods are more appropriate to study the dynamics underling gamma synchronization.
source: Time-resolved non-stationary methods are therefore more appropriate to study the dynamics underling gamma synchronization (Bonizzi et al., 2014; Huang, 2005; Lachaux et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings, supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies have established diversity in the phase-locking of gamma rhythms in the primate visual cortex.
source: Previous studies have established diversity in the phase-locking (Eckhorn et al., 2001; Gray and Singer, 1989; Ray and Maunsell, 2010) and in the phase-relations (Maris et al., 2016; Vinck et al., 2010) of gamma rhythms in the primate visual cortex.
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings, supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies have established diversity in the phase-relations of gamma rhythms in the primate visual cortex.
source: Previous studies have established diversity in the phase-locking (Eckhorn et al., 2001; Gray and Singer, 1989; Ray and Maunsell, 2010) and in the phase-relations (Maris et al., 2016; Vinck et al., 2010) of gamma rhythms in the primate visual cortex.
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings, supported by citations.

claim: How the observed diversity in phase-relation and phase-locking is regulated was not well established before this study.
source: However, how this observed diversity in phase-relation and phase-locking is regulated was not well established.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Mainly two parameters determined gamma synchronization: the detuning Δω and the interaction strength ε.
source: Here, we show that mainly two parameters determined gamma synchronization: the detuning Δω and the interaction strength ε.
evidence: This is a summary statement of a key finding.

claim: Detuning represents a desynchronization force.
source: Detuning represents a desynchronization force, whereas the interaction strength represents a synchronization force.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the role of detuning in synchronization.

claim: The interaction strength represents a synchronization force.
source: Detuning represents a desynchronization force, whereas the interaction strength represents a synchronization force.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the role of interaction strength in synchronization.

claim: In the experiment, detuning was modulated by input drive differences associated with different local contrasts.
source: In our experiment, the former was modulated by input drive differences associated with different local contrasts, and the latter by changes in connectivity strength associated with horizontal cortical distances between electrodes.
evidence: This describes how detuning was manipulated in the experiment.

claim: In the experiment, interaction strength was modulated by changes in connectivity strength associated with horizontal cortical distances between electrodes.
source: In our experiment, the former was modulated by input drive differences associated with different local contrasts, and the latter by changes in connectivity strength associated with horizontal cortical distances between electrodes.
evidence: This describes how interaction strength was manipulated in the experiment.

claim: The interplay of detuning and interaction strength defined the resultant phase-locking strength and the preferred phase-relation between gamma rhythms.
source: Their interplay defined the resultant phase-locking strength and the preferred phase-relation between gamma rhythms.
evidence: This is a summary statement of how the two parameters interact to determine synchronization properties.

claim: The observed role of detuning is in agreement with a previous study in the rat hippocampus.
source: The observed role of detuning is in agreement with a previous study in the rat hippocampus (Akam et al., 2012), in which optogenetic entrainment strength and phase of gamma rhythms were dependent on the frequency-detuning.
evidence: This is a comparison with a previous study, supported by a citation.

claim: The results agree with theoretical concepts of oscillatory interactions.
source: The results also agree with theoretical concepts of oscillatory interactions (Ermentrout and Kopell, 1984a; Hoppensteadt and Izhikevich, 1998; Sancristóbal et al., 2014; Tiesinga and Sejnowski, 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about the agreement of the results with theory, supported by citations.

claim: Small detuning values (mainly <∆10 Hz) and much larger shifts in the gamma frequency-range (25–50 Hz to 65–120 Hz) represent different but complementary mechanisms for controlling gamma synchronization.
source: We suggest that small detuning values (mainly <∆10 Hz) reported in the present study and much larger shifts in the gamma frequency-range (25–50 Hz to 65–120 Hz) as reported in the rat hippocampus (Colgin et al., 2009) represent different but complementary mechanisms for controlling gamma synchronization.
evidence: This is a proposal about the relationship between small and large frequency shifts, supported by a citation.

claim: Only a small difference in gamma frequency will leave a possibility for synchronization while a large difference will preclude synchronization.
source: On the one hand, only a small difference in gamma frequency will leave a possibility for synchronization while a large difference will preclude synchronization.
evidence: This is an explanation of the role of frequency differences in synchronization.

claim: At small levels of detuning that offer opportunities for synchronization, small changes in instantaneous frequency will modulate the exact strength and direction of the gamma-mediated information flow.
source: On the other hand, at small levels of detuning that offer opportunities for synchronization, small changes in instantaneous frequency will modulate the exact strength and direction of the gamma-mediated information flow.
evidence: This is an explanation of the role of instantaneous frequency changes in synchronization.

claim: Instantaneous frequency modulations reflect the overall ability of two cortical locations to engage in gamma-band synchronization.
source: Hence, instantaneous frequency modulations, which define the interaction strength, reflect the overall ability of two cortical locations to engage in gamma-band synchronization.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the meaning of instantaneous frequency modulations.

claim: An important source of instantaneous V1 gamma frequency modulations is the underlying network (intermittent) synchronization process.
source: These modulations are mediated by anatomical connectivity and further modified by oscillation amplitude. Hence, an important source of instantaneous V1 gamma frequency modulations is the underlying network (intermittent) synchronization process, which means that variations in gamma frequencies do not argue against a functional role of gamma synchronization (see Bosman et al., 2009; Burns et al., 2011; 2010; Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the source of frequency modulations, supported by citations.

claim: Variations in gamma frequencies do not argue against a functional role of gamma synchronization.
source: Hence, an important source of instantaneous V1 gamma frequency modulations is the underlying network (intermittent) synchronization process, which means that variations in gamma frequencies do not argue against a functional role of gamma synchronization (see Bosman et al., 2009; Burns et al., 2011; 2010; Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion about the functional implications of frequency variations, supported by citations.

claim: The shape of the instantaneous frequency modulations reflects the underlying interaction function G(θ).
source: Furthermore, we show that the shape of the instantaneous frequency modulations reflects the underlying interaction function G(θ), which in our recording data likely is closely related to the PRC (Hoppensteadt and Izhikevich, 1998; Kopell and Ermentrout, 2002; Kuramoto, 1991; Pikovsky et al., 2002; Winfree, 1967).
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between frequency modulations and the interaction function, supported by citations.

claim: The interaction function describes how the oscillators advance or delay each other's phase development to coordinate their phase-relation.
source: The interaction function describes how the oscillators advance or delay each other's phase development to coordinate their phase-relation.
evidence: This is a definition of the interaction function.

claim: Approximately symmetric sinusoidal-like functions were observed in V1 gamma that resemble the basic function of the widely-used Kuramoto-model.
source: We observed approximately symmetric sinusoidal-like functions in V1 gamma that resemble the basic function of the widely-used Kuramoto-model (Breakspear et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the shape of the observed interaction function and compares it to a known model.

claim: The observed symmetric sinusoidal-like functions are in agreement with the biphasic PRC of gamma rhythms observed in the rat hippocampus.
source: This is in agreement with the biphasic PRC of gamma rhythms observed in the rat hippocampus (Akam et al., 2012) and fits with our observed symmetric Arnold tongues (Izhikevich, 2007; Kopell and Ermentrout, 2002; Pikovsky et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a comparison with a previous study, supported by citations.

claim: The bidirectional interaction function G(θ) was estimated in this study.
source: Importantly, here we estimated the bidirectional interaction function G(θ).
evidence: This describes what was estimated in the study.

claim: The bidirectional interaction function can be symmetric despite the presence of asymmetric individual (unidirectional) PRCs.
source: This function can be symmetric despite the presence of asymmetric individual (unidirectional) PRCs (Cannon and Kopell, 2015; Wang et al., 2013), as long as the rhythms interact approximately equally strongly, which is a plausible assumption between V1 locations.
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between bidirectional and unidirectional interaction functions, supported by citations.

claim: The interaction functions estimated may be smoother than they really are due to limitations of the analysis arising from noise, averaging, and steps taken to reduce volume conduction.
source: The interaction functions we estimated here might be smoother than they really are due to limitations of our analysis arising from noise, averaging, and steps taken to reduce volume conduction.
evidence: This is a statement about potential limitations of the analysis.

claim: Future studies are required to characterize in more detail the (unidirectional/bi-directional) gamma-band interaction functions.
source: Future studies are required to characterize in more detail the (unidirectional/bi-directional) gamma-band interaction functions.
evidence: This is a statement about the need for future research.

claim: Unidirectionally connected neural groups might have asymmetric interaction functions and an asymmetric Arnold tongue.
source: Unidirectionally connected neural groups, for example between certain cortical areas, might have asymmetric interaction functions and an asymmetric Arnold tongue.
evidence: This is a speculation about the properties of unidirectionally connected neural groups.

claim: A frequency difference between cortical areas might be favorable for optimal information transmission in the case of unidirectional connections.
source: In this situation, a frequency difference between cortical areas (Bosman et al., 2012; Cannon et al., 2014) might be favorable for optimal information transmission.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional implications of frequency differences in unidirectionally connected areas, supported by citations.

claim: Synchronization between V1 locations emerged due to mutual horizontal interactions.
source: In addition, we assumed that synchronization between V1 locations emerged due to mutual horizontal interactions, yet common input fluctuations might further shape V1 gamma synchronization (Wang et al., 2000; Wiesenfeld and Moss, 1995; Zhou et al., 2013), especially for neurons with similar receptive fields.
evidence: This is a statement about the assumed mechanism of synchronization, with a caveat about common input.

claim: Common input fluctuations might further shape V1 gamma synchronization, especially for neurons with similar receptive fields.
source: In addition, we assumed that synchronization between V1 locations emerged due to mutual horizontal interactions, yet common input fluctuations might further shape V1 gamma synchronization (Wang et al., 2000; Wiesenfeld and Moss, 1995; Zhou et al., 2013), especially for neurons with similar receptive fields.
evidence: This is a statement about a potential additional mechanism of synchronization, supported by citations.

claim: The observation that gamma synchronization occurred between V1 locations with distinct receptive fields and with a dependence on cortical distance as expected from anatomical connectivity indicates that cross-columnar gamma-band synchronization depends strongly on direct mutual horizontal interactions.
source: Although we did not investigate the possible effects of common input, the observation that gamma synchronization occurred between V1 locations with distinct receptive fields and with a dependence on cortical distance as expected from anatomical connectivity (Gail et al., 2000; Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008; Palanca and DeAngelis, 2005; Ray and Maunsell, 2010; Stettler et al., 2002) indicates that cross-columnar gamma-band synchronization depends strongly on direct mutual horizontal interactions (Veit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference from the observed properties of synchronization, supported by citations.

claim: Detuning was dependent on the local contrast difference.
source: In our experiment, detuning was dependent on the local contrast difference (Ray and Maunsell, 2010; Roberts et al., 2013), known to change neural excitation in V1 (Sclar et al., 1990), while the interaction strength was dependent on the underlying horizontal connectivity strength, here varied by cortical distance (Stettler et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation of detuning, supported by citations.

claim: Local contrast difference is known to change neural excitation in V1.
source: In our experiment, detuning was dependent on the local contrast difference (Ray and Maunsell, 2010; Roberts et al., 2013), known to change neural excitation in V1 (Sclar et al., 1990), while the interaction strength was dependent on the underlying horizontal connectivity strength, here varied by cortical distance (Stettler et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about the effect of contrast on neural excitation, supported by a citation.

claim: The interaction strength was dependent on the underlying horizontal connectivity strength, varied by cortical distance.
source: In our experiment, detuning was dependent on the local contrast difference (Ray and Maunsell, 2010; Roberts et al., 2013), known to change neural excitation in V1 (Sclar et al., 1990), while the interaction strength was dependent on the underlying horizontal connectivity strength, here varied by cortical distance (Stettler et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation of interaction strength, supported by a citation.

claim: Gamma synchronization is informative about the sensory input.
source: Gamma synchronization is therefore informative about the sensory input (Besserve et al., 2015) and about the underlying structure of connectivity.
evidence: This is an inference about the information content of gamma synchronization, supported by a citation.

claim: Gamma synchronization is informative about the underlying structure of connectivity.
source: Gamma synchronization is therefore informative about the sensory input (Besserve et al., 2015) and about the underlying structure of connectivity.
evidence: This is an inference about the information content of gamma synchronization.

claim: The frequency of gamma rhythms is modulated by various sensory stimuli.
source: Indeed, the frequency of gamma rhythms is modulated by various sensory stimuli (Fries, 2015) and by cognitive manipulations (Bosman et al., 2012; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Fries, 2015) suggesting that frequency control is a potential avenue for modulating functional gamma-band coordination and information transfer (Besserve et al., 2015; Buehlmann and Deco, 2010; Lowet et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the modulation of gamma frequency, supported by citations.

claim: The frequency of gamma rhythms is modulated by cognitive manipulations.
source: Indeed, the frequency of gamma rhythms is modulated by various sensory stimuli (Fries, 2015) and by cognitive manipulations (Bosman et al., 2012; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Fries, 2015) suggesting that frequency control is a potential avenue for modulating functional gamma-band coordination and information transfer (Besserve et al., 2015; Buehlmann and Deco, 2010; Lowet et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the modulation of gamma frequency, supported by citations.

claim: Frequency control is a potential avenue for modulating functional gamma-band coordination and information transfer.
source: Indeed, the frequency of gamma rhythms is modulated by various sensory stimuli (Fries, 2015) and by cognitive manipulations (Bosman et al., 2012; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Fries, 2015) suggesting that frequency control is a potential avenue for modulating functional gamma-band coordination and information transfer (Besserve et al., 2015; Buehlmann and Deco, 2010; Lowet et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional implications of frequency modulation, supported by citations.

claim: Detuning may influence the direction of information flow among mutually coupled oscillators.
source: Further, as phase lag is dependent on detuning, detuning may influence the direction of information flow among mutually coupled oscillators.
evidence: This is an inference about the effect of detuning on information flow.

claim: Detuning shapes the information flow between model networks as measured by information theoretical tools.
source: This is in line with granger causality analysis in our paper (Figure 8), but also with network simulations published by us and others (Besserve et al., 2015; Buehlmann and Deco, 2010; Cannon et al., 2014; Lowet et al., 2016) showing that detuning will shape the information flow between model networks as measured by information theoretical tools (e.g. transfer entropy).
evidence: This is a statement about the effect of detuning on information flow, supported by citations and data.

claim: Much more work is needed to explore the influence of detuning on directionality of information flow.
source: Nevertheless, much more work is needed to explore the influence of detuning on directionality of information flow, and the results in the present paper are only suggestive.
evidence: This is a statement about the need for future research.

claim: The effect of detuning on synchronization was strongly modulated by interaction strength.
source: The effect of detuning on synchronization was strongly modulated by interaction strength, which we demonstrated to relate strongly to the strength of horizontal connectivity.
evidence: This is a summary statement of a key finding.

claim: Horizontal connectivity in V1 exhibits remarkable tuning to visual features, orientation being a prime example.
source: Horizontal connectivity in V1 is not only local, but also exhibits remarkable tuning to visual features, orientation being a prime example (Stettler et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of horizontal connectivity, supported by a citation.

claim: Innate and learned connectivity patterns likely affect the interaction strength and hence the synchronization patterns of gamma rhythms within V1.
source: Hence, innate and learned connectivity patterns likely affect the interaction strength and hence the synchronization patterns of gamma rhythms within V1.
evidence: This is an inference about the effect of connectivity patterns on synchronization.

claim: V1 gamma is a functional mechanism for early vision by temporally coordinating local neural activity as a function of sensory input and connectivity.
source: These properties suggest V1 gamma as a functional mechanism for early vision (Eckhorn et al., 2001; Gray and Singer, 1989) by temporally coordinating local neural activity as a function of sensory input and connectivity.
evidence: This is a proposal about the functional role of V1 gamma, supported by citations.

claim: V1 gamma synchronization was found to be mainly local and limited to a narrow range of frequency differences.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Eckhorn et al., 2001; Palanca and DeAngelis, 2005; Ray and Maunsell, 2010), V1 gamma synchronization was found to be mainly local and limited to a narrow range of frequency differences.
evidence: This is a summary statement of a finding, supported by citations.

claim: It is not likely that gamma within V1 'binds' whole perceptual objects.
source: It is therefore not likely that gamma within V1 'binds' whole perceptual objects.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional role of V1 gamma.

claim: V1 gamma is more likely to bind features locally at the level of surround receptive fields.
source: Instead, it is more likely to bind features locally at the level of surround receptive fields.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional role of V1 gamma.

claim: Recent studies on the gamma-band response during natural viewing have found variable levels of synchronization power for different natural images.
source: Furthermore, recent studies on the gamma-band response during natural viewing (Brunet et al., 2015; Hermes et al., 2015) have found variable levels of synchronization power for different natural images.
evidence: This is a statement about recent findings, supported by citations.

claim: The revealed Arnold tongue of V1 gamma implies that natural image parts with high input/detuning variability (heterogeneity) will induce no or weak synchronization.
source: In accordance with these observations, the revealed Arnold tongue of V1 gamma implies that natural image parts with high input/detuning variability (heterogeneity) will induce no or weak synchronization, whereas parts with low input/detuning variability (homogeneity) will induce stronger synchronization.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the Arnold tongue for natural vision.

claim: Natural image parts with low input/detuning variability (homogeneity) will induce stronger synchronization.
source: In accordance with these observations, the revealed Arnold tongue of V1 gamma implies that natural image parts with high input/detuning variability (heterogeneity) will induce no or weak synchronization, whereas parts with low input/detuning variability (homogeneity) will induce stronger synchronization.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the Arnold tongue for natural vision.

claim: The findings are in line with proposals linking gamma synchronization with surround suppression/normalization.
source: This is also in line with proposals linking gamma synchronization with surround suppression/normalization (Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008; Ray et al., 2013) and predictive coding (Vinck and Bosman, 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the agreement of the findings with previous proposals, supported by citations.

claim: The findings are in line with proposals linking gamma synchronization with predictive coding.
source: This is also in line with proposals linking gamma synchronization with surround suppression/normalization (Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008; Ray et al., 2013) and predictive coding (Vinck and Bosman, 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the agreement of the findings with previous proposals, supported by citations.

claim: The mechanism described for gamma synchronization in V1 also holds outside the visual cortex.
source: Finally, we propose that the mechanism we have described for gamma synchronization in V1 also holds outside the visual cortex.
evidence: This is a proposal about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: Gamma synchronization across cortical areas have been observed in spite of frequency differences.
source: Gamma synchronization across cortical areas have been observed in spite of frequency differences (Bosman et al., 2012; Gregoriou et al., 2009), which is further supported by our additional analysis of V1-V2 interactions.
evidence: This is a statement about observations in other cortical areas, supported by citations and data.

claim: Similar principles likely operate for gamma-band inter-areal interactions.
source: Together, this suggests that similar principles likely operate for gamma-band inter-areal interactions.
evidence: This is a speculation about the generalizability of the findings to inter-areal interactions.

claim: Instantaneous gamma frequency fluctuations have been observed in the rat hippocampus.
source: Further, the instantaneous gamma frequency fluctuations that we have shown to be instrumental in regulating synchronization, have also been observed in the rat hippocampus by Atallah and Scanziani (2009).
evidence: This is a statement about observations in the rat hippocampus, supported by a citation.

claim: Instantaneous gamma frequency fluctuations in the rat hippocampus reflected rapid phase shifts due to changes in excitation-inhibition balance.
source: Their analysis suggested that these fluctuations, which reflected rapid phase shifts due to changes in excitation-inhibition balance, might be critical for gamma-mediated information flow.
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of frequency fluctuations in the rat hippocampus, supported by a citation.

claim: Instantaneous frequency modulations during ripples in rodent hippocampus reveal dynamics that may be indicative of processes related to learning and memory.

claim: These findings support the proposal that cycle-by-cycle modulations in frequency that regulate gamma synchronization also happen in other frequency bands and in other brain regions or structures.
source: These findings support our proposal that cycle-by-cycle modulations in frequency that regulate gamma synchronization also happen in other frequency bands and in other brain regions or structures.
evidence: This is a statement about the support for the generalizability of the findings.

evidence: This is a statement about the need for future research.

claim: As long as the instantaneous phase of a neural rhythm can be determined, the methods used in this study can be applied.

evidence: This is a statement about the applicability of the methods.

claim: Instantaneous phase extraction has been applied to theta rhythms.
source: Instantaneous phase extraction has been for example applied to theta rhythms (Belluscio et al., 2012; Buzsáki, 2002) or alpha rhythms (Lakatos et al., 2005; Samaha and Postle, 2015; Schwabedal et al., 2016).

claim: A tight combination of experimental and dynamic systems theory will be critical for fruitful analysis and interpretation of neural oscillatory data.
source: Aside of emerging new technological possibilities for network state modulation, a tight combination of experimental and dynamic systems theory will be critical for fruitful analysis and interpretation of neural oscillatory data.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of combining experimental and theoretical approaches.

claim: The paper offers the first predictive theory of synchronization.
source: In summary, the present paper offers the first predictive theory of synchronization, which we suggest can be used to assess the mechanisms of synchronization in various frequency bands, and to assess their contribution to diverse forms of cognition.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and potential impact of the work.
